name: Kentucky
$methodComment: Structurally fits the existing flatRate() dispatcher (rate applied over annual wages less an annual allowance), but Kentucky's allowance is NOT an employee-chosen exemption count the way flatRate() was built for MI to consume. Form K-4 (42A804, fetched and read directly this session) has NO personal/dependent exemption count field at all -- the $3,360 standard deduction applies once per employee, unconditionally, regardless of dependents. Getting the correct deduction through the existing dispatcher requires the caller to ALWAYS pass workState.certificate.allowances = 1 for a Kentucky employee (never 0, never a real headcount) -- flatRate()'s default of allowances=0 would silently compute a $0 deduction and overwithhold every Kentucky paycheck. This is a real caller footgun, disclosed here rather than silently worked around; PA sidesteps it by setting allowanceAmount=0 (no deduction concept at all), which Kentucky cannot do since it genuinely has a $3,360 deduction.

sources.title: KRS 141.010 -- Definitions for chapter (gross income / adjusted gross income)
sources.verifiedBy: NOT directly fetched this session -- search-summary only. Summary states: KY 'gross income' = IRC Sec 61 gross income; KY 'adjusted gross income' = that gross income minus IRC Sec 62 deductions, 'as modified by KRS 141.0101'. This is the basis for exemptPretax below, but KRS 141.0101's actual modification list was NOT read directly -- one tier below the Indiana IC 6-3-1-3.5 upgrade (full list read, confirmed no add-back) and two tiers below Michigan's RAB-1988-27 (named enumeration). Treat exemptPretax as inferred-from-federal-conformity-structure, not confirmed by a direct read of the modification list itself.

sources.title: Kentucky Raises Unemployment Insurance Wage Base for 2026 (Bloomberg Tax)
sources.verifiedBy: Fetched directly, but this is industry-press REPORTING ON figures attributed to the Kentucky Office of Unemployment Insurance, not a direct fetch of a KY.gov page. Quoted: wage base '$12,000, up from $11,700 for 2025'; new employer '2.7%' ('9%' for contract construction); 'Rate Schedule A contains rates ranging from 0.3% to 2.4% for positive-rated employers and from 6.5% to 9% for negative-rated employers'. One tier below MI/IN's SUTA sourcing, which were direct fetches of the state agency's own page.

flatRate.comment: 3.5% flat rate for 2026, applied to annual wages less the $3,360 standard deduction. Formula and both rate/deduction figures read directly from the DOR's own 2026 Withholding Tax Formula document. HB 8 (2022) set up automatic phased rate cuts gated on state revenue-growth and reserve-fund triggers (path so far: 5% in 2018 (HB 366) -> 4.5% (2023-24) -> 4.0% (2025) -> 3.5% (2026)); further cuts are NOT scheduled/automatic on a calendar, they depend on the trigger being met each year, so this rate should not be assumed to auto-decrement for 2027 without a fresh check.

supplementalComment: NOT a primary-DOR-confirmed figure -- multiple secondary payroll-industry sources (PaycheckCity, Deel, Empower) state Kentucky taxes supplemental wages (bonuses, commissions, severance) at the same flat 3.5% with no separate supplemental provision, which is structurally what you'd expect from a single-rate state with no brackets (there is no second tier for a 'supplemental' rate to diverge into, unlike federal's 22%/37% layered onto a graduated system). The DOR's own 2026 Withholding Tax Formula document does not use the word 'supplemental' anywhere in its own text. Treat this figure as inferred-from-structure plus secondary corroboration, not a named DOR supplemental-wage provision.
exemptComment: INFERRED, not directly confirmed: KRS 141.010 defines KY gross income as IRC Sec 61 gross income and KY AGI as that minus IRC Sec 62 deductions, 'as modified by KRS 141.0101' (search-summary only -- the modification list itself was not fetched this session). Since 401(k)/403(b)/457/SIMPLE elective deferrals and Section 125/132 benefits are already excluded from federal gross income at the point of Form W-2 Box 1 (they are pretax BEFORE Sec 61 gross income is measured, not a Sec 62 'deduction FROM' gross income), a state that starts from federal gross income inherits that exclusion automatically unless it specifically adds the amounts back -- which is exactly the mechanism Kentucky's LOCAL occupational tax uses (see data/local/KY-occupational-2026.json: KRS 67.750(2)(a)-(b) explicitly ADDS these categories back for the local tax base). No equivalent add-back provision was found for the STATE tax in the (search-summary-only) read of KRS 141.010/141.0101. This makes Kentucky STRUCTURALLY like Michigan/Indiana at the STATE level (federal-AGI-conforming, deferrals reduce the base) while being the OPPOSITE at the LOCAL level (deferrals do NOT reduce the base) -- a genuinely new within-one-state split not seen in any other state modelled in this project, and worth a dedicated follow-up read of KRS 141.0101's actual text before trusting this at MI's confidence tier.

withholdingCertificate.$comment: Form K-4 (fetched and read directly). Structurally unlike every other state's withholding certificate modelled in this project: NO personal/dependent exemption count field exists anywhere on the form. Kentucky's standard deduction is a single flat $3,360, identical for every employee regardless of filing status or dependents -- the certificate exists ONLY to claim one of four full-exemption categories, or request additional flat-dollar withholding.

source.title: 42A804 (K-4)(12-2025)
source.verifiedBy: PDF downloaded and read directly this session, both pages.

fields.additionalWithholdingPerPayPeriod: A flat dollar amount, same concept as federal W-4 Step 4(c). NOT currently modelled in the engine (flatRate() has no field for this, same gap as MI/IN's equivalent line).
fields.exemptionClaims: Four checkboxes, ALL-OR-NOTHING (there is no partial-exemption or per-category-count concept the way other states' certificates work):
fields.exemption1_noLiabilityExpected: For 2026: both (a) the employee had a right to a full 2025 refund because they owed zero KY tax, AND (b) they expect a full 2026 refund. Gated on modified-gross-income poverty-level thresholds by family size ($15,650 single / $21,150 family of 2 / $26,650 family of 3 / $32,150 family of 4+, all 2025 figures per the form). Expires 2027-02-15.
fields.exemption2_fortCampbell: Public Law 105-261 -- wages earned AT the Fort Campbell, KY military base are exempt from KY income tax if the employee is a nonresident of Kentucky (residency defined by KRS 141.010(32): domiciled in KY, OR maintains a KY abode and is present 183+ days/year). Must be revoked within 10 days of moving to Kentucky.
fields.exemption3_militarySpouse: Servicemembers Civil Relief Act as amended by the Military Spouses Residence Relief Act. Requires a 6-statement worksheet (spouse is a servicemember with current KY orders, employee is not a servicemember, they share an address, employee is present in KY solely to accompany the spouse, spouse's domicile state is elsewhere and employee elects to use it) all answered YES, plus a copy of the spouse's military photo ID. Terminates on the earliest of: spouse leaves military, employee enlists, they no longer share an address, or spouse's duty station moves outside KY.
fields.exemption4_reciprocalState: See reciprocity below -- this is the SAME form/box that operationalizes 103 KAR 17:140's exemption; a reciprocal-state resident checks this box (with the Virginia-commute / Ohio-S-corp carve-outs applied via the form's own sub-checkboxes) rather than filing a separate document.

withholdingCertificate.employerInstructions: K-4 is required ONLY to document a claimed exemption or a requested additional-withholding amount -- if neither applies, the employer is not required to keep a K-4 on file at all (i.e. the default/no-form case is 'withhold via the standard formula', not 'no withholding'). This is a meaningfully different default than a W-4-style 'no form filed' ambiguity.
withholdingCertificate.knownGap: No certificate field models the additional-withholding dollar amount or any of the four exemption categories in the engine yet -- input.workState.certificate has no Kentucky-specific shape defined in types.ts.

source.title: 103 KAR 17:140 -- Individual income tax - reciprocity - nonresidents
source.verifiedBy: PDF fetched and read directly this session, full regulatory text.

reciprocity.mechanismDiffersFromMIAndOH: Structurally different from every reciprocity relationship already modelled in this project: this is SOURCE-STATE exemption (Kentucky, the WORK state, simply does not tax the nonresident's wages at all), not a residence-based credit or a symmetric two-way rule. 103 KAR 17:140 Section 1 explicitly scopes this to 'the specific types of income listed' -- it says nothing about how KENTUCKY RESIDENTS working in one of these 7 states are treated by Kentucky. Michigan's and Ohio's reciprocity data files both document an explicit two-way symmetric or direction-matters rule read from their own primary source; Kentucky's regulation, as read, only ever addresses the nonresident-working-in-KY direction.
reciprocity.kyResidentWorkingInReciprocalStateNotCon: INFERRED, not confirmed by direct statute read: Kentucky almost certainly still taxes its own residents' worldwide income by default (the standard resident-taxation pattern every other state in this project uses), meaning a KY resident earning wages in, say, Ohio would likely remain KY-taxable on that income (with some form of out-of-state tax credit under KRS 141.070's general resident-credit framework) rather than being exempt the way MI's reciprocity works for its own residents. This is a plausible inference from the general shape of state reciprocity law, NOT something read directly in a Kentucky statute this session -- flagged as an open item rather than asserted.

perStateConditions.IL: Residents of Illinois exempt on wages and salaries. No further condition stated.
perStateConditions.IN: Residents of Indiana exempt on wages, salaries, AND commissions (broader than the other six, which say only 'wages and salaries' / 'personal services').
perStateConditions.MI: Residents of Michigan exempt on income earned from 'personal services' in Kentucky, which the regulation itself defines to include salaries and wages.
perStateConditions.OH: Residents of Ohio exempt on salaries and wages EXCEPT: effective for tax years beginning on/after 2007-01-01, wages an S corporation pays to a shareholder-employee who is a 20%-or-greater direct or indirect equity investor in that S corp are NOT covered by the exemption -- that specific person remains KY-taxable.
perStateConditions.VA: Residents of Virginia exempt ONLY if they commute DAILY to their Kentucky workplace. A Virginia resident who does not commute daily (e.g. works a multi-day-in-KY / return-home-periodically pattern) does not qualify -- the daily-commute condition is load-bearing, not a formality.
perStateConditions.WV: Residents of West Virginia exempt on salaries and wages. No further condition stated.
perStateConditions.WI: Residents of Wisconsin exempt on income earned from 'personal services' in Kentucky (same phrasing/scope as Michigan).

reciprocity.residencyOverride: Section 4: a person domiciled in one of the 7 reciprocal states who ALSO maintains a Kentucky abode and spends more than 183 days/year in Kentucky loses reciprocity entirely and is treated as a Kentucky resident for tax purposes -- same 183-day mechanism used elsewhere in KY law (KRS 141.010(32), also the Fort Campbell exemption's residency test).
reciprocity.mechanism: Employee self-certifies via Form K-4 box 4 (see withholdingCertificate.exemption4_reciprocalState above), filed with and held by the employer. A secondary source (not verified this session) separately referenced 'Form 42A809' as a reciprocity-related form -- possibly a return-side claim for someone who already had KY tax withheld despite qualifying, distinct from K-4's prospective withholding exemption; NOT reconciled this session, flagged rather than guessed at.
reciprocity.underlyingAgreements: Section 5 incorporates seven bilaterally-negotiated agreements by reference, with original execution dates ranging from 1964 (Virginia) to 1972 (Ohio) -- these are old, individually-negotiated treaties, not one uniform multi-state compact, which is consistent with why each state's exact income-type wording differs slightly (Indiana's 'commissions', Michigan/Wisconsin's 'personal services') rather than using one shared clause.
reciprocity.knownGap: Not implemented in the calculation engine -- same as every other state's reciprocity in this project. Additionally, unlike MI/IN, even the DATA side of the KY-resident-outbound direction is unconfirmed (see kyResidentWorkingInReciprocalStateNotConfirmed above), which MI's and IN's files do not have as an open question.

unemploymentInsurance.$comment: Employer-only (SUI) -- no employee contribution, consistent with every other state modelled in this project.

sources.title: Kentucky Raises Unemployment Insurance Wage Base for 2026 (Bloomberg Tax)
sources.verifiedBy: Fetched directly, but this is industry-press reporting attributing figures to the Kentucky Office of Unemployment Insurance -- NOT a direct fetch of a KY.gov page. One tier below MI/IN's SUTA sourcing.

unemploymentInsurance.wageBaseComment: Up from $11,700 in 2025. Two other figures ($11,100, $11,400) surfaced in initial search results and were rejected in favor of $12,000 as the more recent/authoritative figure -- not independently reconciled beyond that judgment call.

rates.scheduleInUse: Schedule A, in effect since 2019 per the source.

unemploymentInsurance.confidence: secondary-sourced (industry press reporting on the state agency's figures), not a direct fetch of a Kentucky Office of Unemployment Insurance page. No trust-fund trigger formula (the mechanism that sets the wage base year to year) was found -- unlike Michigan's SUTA, where the underlying formula was read directly.
unemploymentInsurance.knownGap: Not modelled in the engine -- same structural note as every other state's SUTA in this project: experience-rated, an individual employer's actual rate depends on employer-specific history no static jurisdiction constant can supply. Additionally, unlike MI/IN, this session did not reach a direct primary-source fetch for KY's UI figures at all.

localOccupationalTax.$comment: Kentucky's PA-EIT/OH-municipal equivalent, but structurally distinct from both and the most complex local-tax shape modelled in this project so far -- see the dedicated file for the full writeup.
localOccupationalTax.summary: Cities, counties, AND school districts can each independently levy an occupational license tax on wages/salaries/commissions AND on business net profits, and these can STACK -- but for the 30,000-300,000 population county tier there is a mandatory CITY-TAX-CREDITS-AGAINST-COUNTY-TAX mechanism (KRS 68.197(6)-(7)) rather than simple additive stacking, which most secondary sources describing this tax gloss over. Counties are statutorily rate-capped (population-tiered: 1.25% for the one 300,000+ county, Jefferson/Louisville; 1% for 30,000+); CITIES ARE NOT CAPPED BY STATUTE AT ALL (KRS 92.281 traces city taxing power to the KY Constitution's Section 181 with no numeric ceiling). The taxable-wage BASE definition (KRS 67.750(2)) explicitly ADDS BACK 401(k)/403(b)/457/SIMPLE deferrals and Section 125/132 benefits -- the opposite of this file's own exemptPretax for the STATE tax.
localOccupationalTax.knownGap: Only 2 of an estimated ~300 taxing jurisdictions have any rate data captured (Louisville Metro, Lexington-Fayette) -- see the local file's own knownGaps for the full list of what remains open, including that the engine has no dispatch method at all for this tax shape.

knownGaps: flatRate()'s allowanceAmount x certificate.allowances design assumes an employee-chosen count; Kentucky's $3,360 deduction is unconditional and requires callers to always pass allowances=1 -- see $methodComment above. This is a real integration risk, not just a documentation note.

exemptPretax is inferred from KRS 141.010's federal-AGI-conformity structure, NOT confirmed by a direct read of KRS 141.0101's actual modification list -- one tier below Indiana's confirmed-full-list read.
supplementalRate (3.5%) is inferred from Kentucky's single-flat-rate structure plus secondary corroboration, not a named DOR supplemental-wage provision.
SUTA figures are secondary-sourced (Bloomberg Tax reporting), not a direct fetch of a Kentucky Office of Unemployment Insurance page -- no trust-fund trigger formula found.
Reciprocity's KY-resident-working-in-a-reciprocal-state direction is inferred, not confirmed -- 103 KAR 17:140 as read only addresses the nonresident-working-in-KY direction.
The K-4's own additional-withholding amount and all four exemption-claim categories have zero representation in types.ts's certificate model.
Local occupational tax is understood structurally but almost entirely unenumerated (2 of ~300 jurisdictions) and entirely unwired in the engine -- see data/local/KY-occupational-2026.json.

No computation code path exists in src/taxes/state.ts for KY-specific mechanics beyond what flatRate() already does generically -- this file has not been run through calculatePaycheck() or covered by any test yet, unlike MI/IN which both have hand-derived fixtures proving the engine dispatches correctly. That verification step has not been done this session.
